header: Date: 2026-09-12 | Start: 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~42m | Attendees: Alice Morgan (Redwood AE), Ben Chao (Redwood SE), Jorge Reyes (PeakData CTO), Maya Singh (PeakData ML Eng), Oliver Park (PeakData Cloud Eng)
summary: Redwood AE+SE walked PeakData through Hosted API chat/text generation basics: streaming responses, common generation params, retry/idempotency patterns, and quick notes on security. Customer is evaluating both hosted and dedicated options for a search-assist feature; next steps are pricing, security docs, and POC scoping.
topics: Generation parameters: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences
transcript:
[00:00] Alice (Redwood AE): Hey everyone good afternoon, thanks for joining. I'm Alice, AE for Redwood. With me is Ben, our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Jorge (PeakData CTO): Doing good, thanks. Ready to see what you have.
[00:12] Ben (Redwood SE): Hi folks, I want to set expectations - quick tour of Hosted API for chat and text gen, then demo streaming and param tuning, finish with retries and some Q&A.
[00:20] Maya (PeakData ML): Sounds good. We're mainly focused on a search-assist use case where we need low latency completion and controllable output.
[00:27] Alice: Perfect - that'll drive a lot of the convo. Oliver, you're on infra?
[00:30] Oliver (Cloud Eng): Yep, I'll be listening for auth, VPC, and region bits.
[00:33] Ben: Cool. I'll start by showing a simple chat payload. Note preface: our Hosted API supports streaming responses so clients can render tokens as they arrive, that helps with perceived latency.
[00:44] Ben: (share screen) Here's a sample curl and a small node example. We call POST /v1/chat with messages array, model param, and streaming enabled via SSE or chunked JSON.
[00:55] Speaker 1: there's a little typo in the demo doc - it says stream=true but we actually use stream: sse in our SDK examples sometimes so watch for that.
[01:05] Jorge: When you say streaming, is that server-sent events or websockets?
[01:09] Ben: Primarily SSE for the HTTP path; we also support websocket endpoints for high-throughput streaming in Dedicated. For Hosted API standard SSE is the common pattern.
[01:18] Maya: How do you handle partial tokens and reconstructing on client side? Any heuristics?
[01:22] Ben: We emit delta tokens with sequence numbers. Clients should assemble in order; we include end_of_stream flag. Edge case: network retries might produce duplicates so we recommend idempotency keys.
[01:33] Alice: Quick note - for idempotency you send idempotency_key in the header, if the request times out clients can retry safely within retention window.
[01:42] Oliver: What's that retention window?
[01:44] Ben: By default four hours for hosted, can be adjusted for Dedicated agreements. We'll also show retry recommendations below.
[01:50] Jorge: Latency numbers - for small responses we need p95 < 200ms, is that realistic with streaming?
[01:55] Ben: For short completions yes - streaming helps perceived latency. Our benchmarks show p95 ~150-220ms for base models on hosted in our nearest region, but depends on prompt size and KV cache hit rates.
[02:09] Maya: KV cache - you mean prefix and kv cache? How transparent is that?
[02:13] Ben: Right, we have prefix caching and KV cache for autoregressive states. It's automatic; you can pin cache keys for reuse across requests. There are TTLs and eviction policies.
[02:22] Jorge: That sounds useful for chat turn continuity.
[02:25] Ben: Exactly. Now params - common knobs are temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences. We'll demo how changing temperature affects randomness.
[02:35] (screen: interactive demo)
[02:38] Ben: Low temp like 0.0 outputs deterministic responses; 0.7 gives more variety. For your search-assist, mid-low temps usually balance helpfulness and safety.
[02:48] Maya: We need to add guardrails around hallucinations - stop sequences and safety filters?
[02:53] Alice: We do have safety classification pipelines and you can set response filters and post-processing rules. For PII, you can route through private deployment or use redact-on-ingest patterns.
[03:04] Jorge: On the hosted side, how do you handle data retention and logs? We're sensitive to query contents.
[03:09] Alice: Hosted keeps minimal logs for billing and debugging; you can opt-out of retention, or route sensitive workloads to Dedicated or Private where you control retention. We'll share SOC 2 docs and network diagrams.
[03:20] Oliver: What's the auth story - API keys only or SSO for teams?
[03:24] Alice: For Hosted API, API keys and org-level SSO for console access. Dedicated/Private supports customer-managed KMS and SAML/SSO at scale.
[03:32] Ben: Back to retries - recommended pattern: exponential backoff with jitter, include idempotency key. For non-idempotent operations like streaming partials, it's trickier; we recommend checkpointing at known boundaries.
[03:46] Maya: If a stream drops mid-response and we retry, will we get duplicate tokens?
[03:50] Ben: Potentially; client-side dedupe by sequence id is safest. We include chunk ids in each SSE message.
[03:57] Jorge: Any rate limits we should expect?
[04:00] Alice: Hosted has tiered rate limits based on plan; we can increase limits for Pilot/MVP. Dedicated gives you reserved throughput with SLA.
[04:09] (paper rustling)
[04:12] Ben: Now I'll run a quick end-to-end request - single-shot prompt, stream on. Watch token events appear in the console.
[04:20] Ben: (typing) ...sending...
[04:28] Ben: You can see chunks with token deltas, cumulative text, and finalization event. If you look at headers, there's x-request-id and idempotency-key echo.
[04:40] Maya: Nice. How about retry-able status codes? 429, 5xx?
[04:44] Ben: 429 for rate limiting, 5xx for server issues. 500s are transient usually. Client should implement backoff and consider fallback to a smaller model or cached response for critical flows.
[04:56] Jorge: Do you have automatic fallback policies?
[04:58] Alice: Yes, in the Console you can configure routing policies - region fallback, model variant fallback, and capacity-tier fallback.
[05:06] Oliver: Any notes on cost math - streaming tokens vs non-streaming?
[05:10] Ben: Tokens billed are the same; streaming just changes delivery. Cost drivers remain model size, token count, and context window. For cost/perf we often recommend quantized variants for Dedicated.
[05:21] Maya: We're curious about SDKs - do you have official Node/Python SDKs?
[05:24] Alice: Yes both, plus Go examples. We'll send sample repos.
[05:28] Ben: Also a bunch of quickstart templates for chat agents and reranking.
[05:32] Jorge: Any gotchas with stop sequences in multilingual prompts?
[05:36] Ben: Stop sequences are literal; for multilingual you may need multiple stop tokens. You can also provide structured output with json schema enforcement which helps.
[05:46] Maya: Can you show structured output enforcement?
[05:49] Ben: Sure - (demo) we request a JSON schema and the model tries to conform, plus the API returns a schema_validation flag when it's not confident. It's heuristics not perfect but useful for extraction tasks.
[06:04] Jorge: On benchmarking - can you run our prompt set to give latency+cost estimates?
[06:08] Alice: Absolutely - that's part of POC scoping. If you send prompt set and expected QPS, Ben's team will run a sample benchmark.
[06:16] Maya: QPS will be bursty, mix of short completions and some long generation. Goal is p95 < 300ms for short ones.
[06:24] Ben: We'll advise batching strategies and cache hints. Sometimes combining small prompts into a batching window hits throughput sweet spot but can hurt tail latency. We'll show tradeoffs.
[06:36] Jorge: Security review we need - SOC 2, ISO, encryption at rest, KMS integration.
[06:42] Alice: We'll attach our long-form security pack. Dedicated supports customer KMS so keys never land on our side. For Hosted, we use provider KMS with envelope encryption; we can discuss contractual terms.
[06:55] Oliver: Network-wise we might prefer VPC peering or private link.
[06:59] Alice: We support PrivateLink and VPC peering patterns; for heavy regulated workloads we recommend Private deployment.
[07:06] Maya: For the POC, what's the timeline to spin up a dedicated trial?
[07:10] Alice: For a small pilot, we can do hosted pilot within days. Dedicated pilot usually takes a couple of weeks for provisioning and validation.
[07:18] Ben: I'll follow up with a checklist for sample data, target SLAs, and test harness.
[07:25] Jorge: Great. A few quick clarifying questions: streaming is SSE, idempotency keys recommended, duplicates possible, use seq ids. Check.
[07:33] Ben: Yup. Also for deterministic answers set temperature=0 and consider logprobs for confidence scoring.
[07:40] Maya: How do you recommend handling partial generation failures in client UX?
[07:44] Alice: Show partial content and a loading state; if finalization fails show a "try again" CTA that replays from last checkpoint using idempotency.
[07:53] Jorge: Any competitors we should watch?
[07:55] Alice: Customers sometimes evaluate OpenAI, Anthropic, and cloud vendors like Vertex AI for tight infra integration. We'll share a comparative note.
[08:06] (some side conversation)
[08:12] Ben: Last bit - retries: 429 -> backoff; 5xx -> exponential backoff up to N tries (we recommend 3), include jitter, and monitor throttles. For streams, try to recover using tokens checkpointed server-side when available.
[08:29] Maya: Are logs searchable in the Console? Can we tag requests?
[08:33] Alice: Yes Console has request-level logs with tag metadata; retention depends on plan. You can also export logs to your SIEM.
[08:44] Jorge: Okay that covers most of our concerns. Next steps?
[08:48] Alice: We'll send pricing, SOC2/security pack, and sample SDK examples. We'll also schedule POC scoping.
[08:56] Ben: I'll attach benchmark checklist and sample curl/node/python snippets.
[09:00] Maya: I'll send prompt corpus and expected throughput numbers.
[09:04] Oliver: I'll review network diagram requirements for PrivateLink.
[09:09] Alice: Great - thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the scoping call.
[09:15] Jorge: Appreciate it, thanks all.
[09:18] (call ends)

Notes: transcript contains occasional small transcription errors (e.g., "stream: sse" vs "stream=true" in docs), and speaker tags were manually aligned.
